title: Game Over: TOJam 2012

contributors.contribution: Created a small number of graphics, including the title-screen artwork.

description: For TOJam 2012's theme, 'The World is NOT Ending,' I created Game Over, a 2D RPG where the hero has already defeated the final boss and saved the world. The new challenge is simply keeping him from getting bored while completing everyday quests for the King. Built over a weekend in my Java C.E.L.L. engine, the game combined quests, AI, scripted triggers, tile-based exploration, a boredom-pressure mechanic, and a procedurally generated overworld that I refined and completed using my visual editor.

sections.title: The World is NOT Ending
paragraphs: The TOJam theme was 'The World is NOT Ending.'
I inverted the usual RPG structure by starting after the dramatic part was already over: the hero had defeated the final boss and saved the world.

sections.title: Game Over
paragraphs: The game was titled Game Over.
With no apocalypse left to stop, the hero's new problem is boredom.

sections.title: Everyday Hero Quests
paragraphs: The King assigns deliberately mundane post-adventure quests to keep the hero occupied.

sections.title: Bored Meter
paragraphs: A visible Bored Meter provided the game's central pressure mechanic.
The joke and gameplay both revolve around completing enough ordinary tasks to keep a legendary hero occupied after his great adventure is already finished.

sections.title: Weekend Development
paragraphs: I built the game mostly myself over the TOJam weekend.
Because C.E.L.L. already provided the reusable engine foundation, the jam work focused on the game-specific world, menus, quests, AI, scripting, and artwork.

sections.title: C.E.L.L. Engine
paragraphs: Game Over was built using my C.E.L.L. Java game engine.
At the time, C.E.L.L. already provided the standard systems I needed for rapid 2D game production.

sections.title: Layered Map & Event Architecture
paragraphs: The game world used separate data layers for visual tiles, foreground/overlay tiles, collision, and scripted actions.
A dedicated event mask triggered scripted game actions when the player entered specific tiles.

sections.title: Scripted World Transitions
paragraphs: Action-map tiles connected the generated overworld to authored locations including the castle, basement, town, store, and caves.
The same event system drove quest interactions such as the King, cat, keys, milk, and boredom-related messages.

sections.title: World Entities & AI
paragraphs: The finished world contained multiple independently configured entity types with their own animation, collision, movement, and AI behaviors.

sections.title: Java2D & Audio
paragraphs: The Java version of the engine used Java2D for rendering.
JavaZoom was used for MP3 playback.

sections.title: Cross-Platform Engine Lineage
paragraphs: The engine architecture was intentionally kept basic enough to maintain parallel implementations for other platforms.
At the time I also had related C.E.L.L. implementations targeting XNA, Android, and BlackBerry.

sections.title: Procedural World Generation
paragraphs: I procedurally generated the initial world-map topology using a cellular-automata cave-generation technique that I found on RogueBasin and translated/adapted into Java.
The cave-generation algorithm itself was third-party/reference material; my work was the Java adaptation and the larger world-generation and authoring pipeline built around it.

sections.title: Cellular Automata Configuration
paragraphs: The generator began with randomly seeded floor/wall cells and applied cellular-automata smoothing.

sections.title: 128 x 128 Tile World
paragraphs: The generated maps were 128 x 128 tiles.
Individual tiles were 64 x 50 pixels, making the resulting world relatively large for the mobile-oriented engine generation.

sections.title: BMP Tile-Map Encoding
paragraphs: I saved the generated floor/wall values into a BMP and used pixel values as tile IDs.
Using a 24-bit BMP provided a very large theoretical tile-ID range while keeping the map file compact; this game used roughly 90 tile types.

sections.title: Separate Collision Map
paragraphs: I maintained collision data in a separate BMP rather than deriving collision directly from the visual tile map.
This allowed visual presentation and walkability rules to evolve independently.

sections.title: Terrain Post-Processing
paragraphs: After generating the initial floor/wall topology, I post-processed the map to turn the raw binary result into a more natural overworld.
items: Replace adjacent land with appropriate shoreline/border tile values
Convert regions into marshland and other terrain

sections.title: Generate, Select, Edit
paragraphs: I repeatedly generated worlds until I found an interesting layout rather than treating the first random result as final.
Once I selected a good world, I opened it in my GUI editor and continued authoring it by hand.

sections.title: Visual World Editing
paragraphs: The generated map became the foundation rather than the finished level.
I used the C.E.L.L. GUI editor to add and refine authored gameplay areas such as towns, castles, paths, entrances, and other level details.

sections.title: Trigger / Action Map
paragraphs: In addition to the visual map and collision map, I maintained another map for scripted trigger actions.
Walking over a trigger tile could execute an action script, such as warping the player from the exterior castle door to the interior castle map.

sections.title: Scripted RPG Structure
paragraphs: The game combined tile-based exploration with scripted transitions, quests, AI, menus, and RPG-style interfaces.
The map-generation system and editor provided the world, while C.E.L.L.'s scripting and trigger systems connected that world into playable quest logic.

sections.title: Artwork & Music
paragraphs: I created most of the game's artwork and UI during the weekend.
A friend contributed the music, and another friend created a small number of graphics including the title screen.

sections.title: Completed & Distributed
paragraphs: Game Over was completed as a playable TOJam submission.
I publicly shared both a gameplay video and a downloadable build after the event.

sections.title: 10-Minute Boredom Clock
paragraphs: The Bored Meter is a real timed lose condition rather than just a visual joke.
The game gives the player approximately 10 minutes to complete the remaining quests before the hero becomes completely bored and the game ends.

sections.title: Three Main Quests
paragraphs: The submitted game contains three tracked quests, each removed from the quest list when completed.
items: Clean Basement: find and defeat all 4 rats
Make Dinner: collect 3 fish, 1 mushroom, 3 chickens, and 1 milk
Find the King's Cat: locate the cat hidden in a maze of trees

sections.title: Projectile Combat
paragraphs: The player has a directional projectile attack implemented through a reusable pool of 50 projectiles.
The attack is used against hostile creatures such as basement rats and mushroom enemies.

sections.title: Post-Game RPG Parody
paragraphs: The inventory, magic, status, and quest systems deliberately parody an overpowered RPG hero who has already completed the important adventure.
The hero begins with legendary equipment, huge supplies, and exaggerated magic while the actual remaining objectives are chores such as catching chickens and buying milk.

historicalNotes: The legacy portfolio card was titled 'ToJam (2012)'; the actual game title was Game Over.
Canonical public title should be 'Game Over: TOJam 2012'.
The TOJam theme was 'The World is NOT Ending'.
The game premise begins after the hero has already defeated the final boss and saved the world.
The player completes mundane quests to keep the hero occupied and prevent boredom.
Known quests included fishing, cleaning the basement, finding the King's missing cat, and making the King's dinner.
Jamie built the game mostly himself over the weekend.
One friend created the music.
Another friend created a small number of graphics, including the title screen.
Jamie created most of the remaining art and UI.
The game used Jamie's C.E.L.L. Java engine.
Jamie's contemporary 2012 description of C.E.L.L. listed sprite animation, collision detection, input, scripting, tiles, sounds, and GUI editing.
The Java engine used Java2D and JavaZoom for MP3 playback.
Jamie also maintained related C.E.L.L. implementations targeting XNA, Android, and BlackBerry.
The procedural-generation seed algorithm came from the RogueBasin cellular-automata cave-generation tutorial/reference and was translated/adapted to Java by Jamie.
Do not publicly imply that Jamie invented the underlying cellular-automata cave algorithm.
Jamie's original Java configuration used fillprob 0.40f, one generation configuration, r1_cutoff 5, r2_cutoff 2, and reps 3.
The generated maps were 128 x 128 tiles.
Tiles were 64 x 50 pixels.
The visual tile map was stored in a 24-bit BMP.
Jamie noted that 24-bit encoding allowed a huge theoretical number of tile IDs, though the game used approximately 90.
A separate BMP stored collision information.
A separate map also stored scripted trigger/action information.
Jamie post-processed generated water boundaries into shoreline/border tile IDs.
Interior water regions could be transformed into terrain such as trees, cliffs, marshland, and related map features.
Jamie repeatedly generated maps until he found an interesting layout.
The selected procedural map was then opened in Jamie's GUI editor for manual level authoring.
Castles, towns, paths, and other authored locations were added after procedural generation.
Trigger tiles could execute scripts such as warping the player through a castle entrance into an interior map.
Game Over was publicly shared through a YouTube gameplay video and downloadable S3 build.
The downloadable build was historically hosted at https://s3.amazonaws.com/SquareParticle/gameover.zip.
The gameplay video was historically posted at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=H3M4sNgcqJ0.
CaveGen should be treated primarily as a subsystem/tool within this project rather than a standalone invention card unless intentionally showcased separately.
This is the correct project lineage for CaveGen; it should not be associated with ShaderBox or the MolyJam 2013 voxel game.
Surviving C.E.L.L. scripts confirm four map-data layers: base visual map, overlay visual map, collision map, and event/action map.
Surviving scripts confirm authored transitions to castle, basement, town, store, cave, and other interior areas.
Entity scripts confirm dedicated AI types for rats, hostile mobs, mushroom enemies, chickens, fish, and mushrooms.
Quest/event scripts reference the King, cat, keys, milk, flowers, boredom, basement, cave, town, and store interactions.
The game configuration explicitly loads gamemusic.mp3 as its main music track.
Input mappings were data-driven through C.E.L.L. script configuration rather than being embedded only in game-specific code.
